Claude Math Breakthrough


# Anthropic Mathematician Uses Claude to Prove the Riemann Hypothesis


By OpenTools Team


·


November 21, 2026


Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, claims to have proved the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. The proof is formalized in Lean but remains unverified. The announcement comes amid an AI‑driven transformation of mathematics.


## A Claim That Would Reshape Mathematics


On Friday,[Anthropic](https://opentools.ai/organizations/anthropic) mathematician **Levent Alpoge posted a four-page note to his personal website** that could change the course of mathematics. He wrote: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,[in a statement](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) that ricocheted through the AI and mathematics communities within hours.


The Riemann Hypothesis, proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely considered the most important unsolved problem in pure mathematics. It is one of seven **Millennium Prize problems** designated by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a $1 million reward. Only one (the Poincare conjecture) has been solved so far,[The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1010051/anthropic-riemann-hypothesis-millennium-prize-problem) reported.


Alpoge claims the method extends beyond the original hypothesis to resolve the **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** as well, and he expects to reach the Extended Riemann Hypothesis with more time.


## A 250,000-Page AI-Generated Proof


There is no traditional paper. Instead, Alpoge released the proof as a **Lean formalization** — 14 compressed archive files in the Lean programming language and proof assistant, which checks mathematical reasoning step by step. The AI-generated informal writeup, he noted, ran past **250,000 pages** ,[MLQ.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/anthropic-mathematician-levent-alpoge-posts-a-claimed-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis-made-with-claude/) reported.


It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of slop, I decided to only present Lean, Alpoge wrote. He ackowledged that the argument remains extraordinarily long and difficult to read,[IBM](https://www.ibm.com/think/news/anthropic-claude-riemann-hypothesis-math-proof) noted.


Alpoge described Claudes role in vivid terms: This time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line, he wrote, adding that he guided us to the right situation before Claude began to leave me in awe. Claude suggested building the crucial mathematical multiplicity from a chain of theta lifts, with the chains length growing like the square root of the size of the primes being counted.


## Awkward Timing and a Broadening AI Math Wave


The announcement landed one day after[Anthropics](https://opentools.ai/tools/anthropics) record-breaking IPO on Nasdaq — a coincidence Alpoge directly addressed. The precise timing is horrible, he wrote. The result came together late Sunday night and he messaged CEO Dario Amodei about announcing it, noting there was a constraint to respect. He insisted the timing was not staged: There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false.


The claim is part of a broader wave of AI-driven mathematical breakthroughs. In September,[OpenAI](https://opentools.ai/organizations/openai) claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem using 10,000 Codex agents, though that claim remains unverified. Alpoge himself previously claimed a Claude-generated disproof of the Jacobian conjecture in July,[The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1010051/anthropic-riemann-hypothesis-millennium-prize-problem) reported.


Anthropics own earlier stance adds tension: in August, the company published research showing Claude raised the known bound on zeta zeros from 41.6% to 67.2%, but explicitly said they expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis, according to[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta) .


## What Builders Should Know About Lean and Formal Verification


The choice of Lean is significant for developers. Lean is not just an academic tool — it is a programming language and interactive theorem prover that **checks every logical step mechanically** . A proof that compiles in Lean is, in principle, as reliable as a program that compiles and passes all tests. The fact that Alpoge chose Lean over a traditional paper reflects a growing trend toward machine-verifiable mathematics.


For builders working with AI code generation, this is a powerful signal: Claude was able to generate and formalize a proof of enormous complexity — one that, if verified, would be among the greatest mathematical achievements in history. It suggests AI systems are approaching a level of reasoning that could transform software verification, cryptographic protocols, and formal methods.


The immediate practical takeaway: **Claudes reasoning capabilities are advancing rapidly** . If Claude can contribute to solving the Riemann Hypothesis, its ability to reason about complex codebases, system architectures, and mathematical models is likely far beyond what most developers have tested.


## Expert Caution and What Comes Next


No outside mathematician has yet verified the proof. The Lean archives must be checked for build correctness, axiom choices, and whether the final theorem faithfully states the Riemann Hypothesis. The Clay Mathematics Institute requires **journal publication and at least two years of scrutiny** before awarding the $1 million prize,[per its rules](https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/rules/) .


Alpoge himself is cautious. He admits he may have baked lots of strange suboptimal choices into the argument and expects much shorter proofs to follow. He thanked mathematicians including Manjul Bhargava and Peter Sarnak — though being thanked does not mean they have verified the proof,[MLQ.ai](https://mlq.ai/news/anthropic-mathematician-levent-alpoge-posts-a-claimed-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis-made-with-claude/) noted.


The mathematical community is now in an position without precedent: evaluating a 250,000-page AI-generated proof of humanitys most famous unsolved problem, formalized in code rather than prose. Whether it holds up or not, the process itself signals that the era of AI-assisted mathematical discovery is here.
